Autoresearch

Turn Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an engine that keeps improving your code without stopping.

It is based on Karpathy's autoresearch: a constraint, a mechanical metric, and autonomous iteration add up to gains that compound.

"Set the GOAL → The agent runs the LOOP → You wake up to results"

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that keeps running.

Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse are all supported for the core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification. Hook guardrails ship for two of them: Claude Code, through its native hooks, and pi, through extension events.

Fork-and-flush lets metric loops get past plateaus, following the approach of Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447). At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks branches with fresh context from the best commit so far. Each branch runs briefly, and the winner is kept. Half the branches choose their own ideas, which adds randomness. The other half each receive a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it tries FORK before giving up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

bumblebee

Bumblebee is a read-only tool that collects inventory of package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers one narrow supply-chain response question. When an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines have a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs something else: the messy local state spread across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee reads that scattered on-disk state and writes it out as structured NDJSON component records. Give it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches. That makes for quick, read-only exposure checks when responders already know what they are looking for.

CLI Printing Press

Time and money matter more than anything else. For AI agents, those translate to speed and token spend. A well-designed CLI works like muscle memory for an agent. It doesn't have to dig through docs or take wrong turns, so it burns fewer tokens. We built the Printing Press to print the best CLIs in the world for agents.

The press reads the official API docs and studies every popular community CLI and MCP server. It also sniffs the web for APIs nobody published, such as Google Flights or Dominos. Then it applies the power-user playbook Peter Steinberger proved with discrawl and gogcli: local SQLite, compound commands, and agent-native flags. It combines all of that and prints three things for any API or website: a token-efficient Go CLI, a Claude Code skill, and an MCP server.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across many domains. It measures how much better a model solves complex real-world tasks when it has specialized Skills available.

Production environments often have many Skills installed at once, so we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In the original setup, each task comes with only the one specialized Skill built for it. In our version, every task runs in a global environment that contains all 195 specialized Skills, and all other experimental conditions stay the same. The goal is to see whether an agent can find, choose, and coordinate the relevant Skills from a large installed pool on its own, then arrange them into a workflow that completes the task.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench ( with DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Against the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points. It also cut token consumption by 29.6% and tool calls by 33.1%.

sem tells you which entities changed (functions, methods, classes) rather than which lines.

Releases

sem is a semantic version control tool that runs on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, pulls out every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs at that level. You see "function blahh was modified" in place of "lines x-y changed."

It works in any Git repo and needs no setup.

Cloud-backed queries are opt-in for each repo. Logging in does not upload a repo or send a query. The cloud consent flow documents the public and private repo states, the preview screen, the local audit log, and the forget controls.

Grounded Docs builds a documentation index for your AI coding assistant that matches the library versions you actually use. IWE: a Markdown knowledge base you and your AI agent work on together

Your notes are your agent's memory. IWE is where you work on them together.

Too many AI conversations start from zero. You explain your project, your decisions and your reasoning, and in the next session you explain it all again. Meanwhile your own notes sit somewhere else, where the agent can't reach them.

Sometimes it's worse. The agent "remembers" something in its own internal memory, but you can't easily see what it saved or fix what it got wrong. That memory also stays behind when you switch to the other agents you work with.

IWE gives you and your AI agents one shared place to work, inside your project. It's a folder of connected Markdown documents: specs, plans, decisions, and more. Keep your own ideas there, ask your agent to save what the two of you learn, and come back to that context as the work grows. You can read, edit and organize the documents yourself, and they stay yours.
